newsitem.title: UK: British police scour race track after bomb scare.
newsitem.headline: British police scour race track after bomb scare.

text.p: Police searched thousands of cars stranded at Britain's Aintree racecourse on Sunday, one day after a suspected IRA bomb scare wrecked the 150th Grand National.

Officials were due to decide later on Sunday whether the premier horse race of the sporting calendar -- which attracts millions of bets and thousands of punters -- could be re-staged on Monday. An early evening re-run of the race was expected.

Political condemnation of the bomb scare that forced the abandonment of Saturday's race and the hasty evacuation of tens of thousands of people from the course, in the northwestern city of Liverpool, was quick and universal.

Prime Minister John Major said he had "no doubt" the Irish Republican Army (IRA), fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland, was to blame for the spectacular bomb scare and that such disruptions would only hinder the peace process.
"These people are murderers. They have murdered before. They will murder again, and people ought not to take these threats lightly," Major told BBC television.
He said such attacks, following a spate of similar scares at major road and rail points, would only hurt efforts by the IRA's political allies Sinn Fein to get back into the peace talks.

In Liverpool more than 1,400 people were forced to spend Saturday night sleeping on floors next to strangers, in hostels and leisure centres -- wherever they could find an empty corner out of the harsh and blustery weather.
One couple slept in a hotel sauna, another racegoer in the stable lads' hostel on the course.
"The public were ringing in with offers," said an employee at Liverpool's social services department. "I think some pubs and clubs were open all night to try and help out."
Princess Anne, horse-loving daughter of Queen Elizabeth, and Oscar-winning actor Gregory Peck, were among the punters who fell victim to one of the biggest evaucations in sporting history.
Twenty-four hours after the scare, an estimated 40,000 people remained locked out of their vehicles as the security checks continued.

Increased security measures were expected close by at Anfield soccer ground, where Liverpool were to play Coventry City on Sunday in a Premier League match, and at Wembley stadium in north London for the League Cup final.
"Our advice to fans is to be extra vigilant, the same sort of advice we give to anyone in London in the current climate of possible terrorist activity," said a police spokesman in London.
At Aintree, race-goers hoped to reclaim their cars and head home but the process promised to be long as police and technical units searched every one of the estimated 7,000 vehicles.
Police carried out three controlled explosions on suspicious objects after the two coded bomb warnings wrecked Saturday's race, but said all proved to be harmless.
Major warned Britain that the lack of actual bombs or injuries should not be allowed to breed complacency.
"There's a great danger that people will be lulled into a false sense of security and then there will be a bomb," Major said on BBC television's Breakfast with Frost show.
With many Britons long used to security alerts and bomb scares, the chief concern of many race-goers was their bets.
An estimated $120 million is bet on the Grand National each year and Saturday was no exception.
Bookmakers said bets would stand in the hope the race would be re-run, but that refunds could probably be arranged.
